title: Choice Is the Key to Life Satisfaction — Study
paragraphs: What makes people satisfied with their lives? Many people might say that the answer is feeling happy most of the time. However, a recent study suggests that the freedom to make your own choices may be even more important.

The study, which was published in The Journal of Positive Psychology, was led by Jason Payne, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Psychology at Simon Fraser University in Canada. The researchers surveyed more than 1,200 adults in Canada and the United Kingdom.

Participants answered questions about their positive and negative emotions and how satisfied they were with their lives in general. They were also asked about three basic psychological needs. The first was autonomy, which means feeling free to make your own choices. The second was competence, or feeling capable, and the third was relatedness, which means feeling connected to other people. The researchers then used advanced statistical methods to find out which of these factors best predicted life satisfaction.

As expected, emotions were strongly linked to happiness. However, the researchers found that autonomy predicted life satisfaction even better than emotions did. In fact, autonomy was the only one of the three psychological needs that explained something that feelings alone could not. Even when the researchers took people's positive and negative emotions into account, those who felt more in control of their choices still tended to be more satisfied with their lives.
According to Payne, the results suggest that people are not merely hedonists, meaning that they do not live only for pleasure.

The researchers believe the findings could be useful for employers and governments. They suggest that programs that make people feel good but limit their freedom to choose could actually lower people's overall satisfaction with their lives.

It is worth noting that all of the participants came from Canada and the UK, so the results may not apply to people everywhere. Other research has suggested that the link between autonomy and happiness is stronger in wealthier and more individualistic countries.
